rows.text: So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That’s a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn’t even bother with that, because whatever they tell you today, the law can change tomorrow. I’d assume that what you tell won’t be completely confidential, especially if it sounds like something dangerous. You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

rows.text: My father used to tell suicidal people, “Oh, you want to kill yourself? That’s wonderful. Now you can change what you’ve always been too afraid to change in your life, and then see if you still want to end it!” His point wasn’t that dying is wonderful. If everything’s already on the table, what’s the change you still can’t bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving? Telling your family who you really are? Those aren’t free, and you can’t always take them back, but they’re smaller than dying. Look at that life you’ve been afraid to change while you still have a human body.
